name: Hike
epitaph: Lost to WhatsApp. Then lost to the law.
oneLiner: India's homegrown chat app with stickers, which later became Rush, an app for playing ludo and carrom for cash prizes.
causeOfDeath: Its messaging app could not beat WhatsApp, and its second life in real-money gaming was wiped out when India banned online money games in 2025.
moneyNote: Raised: Inc42's database lists $261 M+ across 8 rounds (TechCrunch said $250 M+ by 2016). Peak: $1.4 bn in the August 2016 round, as confirmed by the founder. End value: the Hike brand and app were later sold to a UK company; no price was published. FY23 figures are in ₹ crore as filed.
inOneMinute: Hike hit **100 million registered users** and a $1.4 billion valuation in 2016, as India's answer to WhatsApp.
Messaging never beat WhatsApp, so Hike shut its chat app in 2021 and **bet on Rush, a real-money gaming app**.
Rush made **$500 million+ in gross revenue**, then a 2025 law banned online money games. Hike closed in September 2025.
killerLine: If one law can switch off your business, **you don't own your future**. Price regulatory risk in before you pivot into it.

chapters.title: The idea
chapters.body: Kavin Bharti Mittal, son of Airtel founder Sunil Bharti Mittal, launched Hike in December 2012. India was just coming online on cheap smartphones. Hike was built for young Indians: **over 80% of its early users were under 25**. It offered free chat, fun Indian stickers, hidden chats for privacy, and free SMS for friends without data. In April 2014 it raised $14 million from BSB, a joint venture between Mittal and SoftBank, after tripling to about 15 million users in nine months. Mittal saw the size of what lay ahead: "There are still less than 100 million active mobile Internet users in India, out of a population of 1.2 billion people."

chapters.title: The rise
chapters.body: Hike grew fast. Tiger Global led a $65 million round in 2014. By January 2016 it had **100 million registered users**, and in August 2016 Tencent and Foxconn led a **$175 million round at a $1.4 billion valuation**. Total funding passed $250 million. Hike was handling 40 billion messages a month and adding games, news and coupons, with payments planned. It wanted to be India's 'super app' (one app for everything, like China's WeChat). Mittal insisted the giant was not his rival: "Hike doesn't even compete with WhatsApp today, it is used very actively in addition to other apps." But WhatsApp already had more than 100 million active users in India.

chapters.title: The cracks
chapters.body: Registered users are not active users. Many people tried Hike, then went back to where their family and friends were: WhatsApp. This is the **network effect** (an app becomes more useful the more of your contacts use it), and it worked against Hike. In January 2019 Hike dropped its super-app plan and split into smaller apps, including Hike Sticker Chat. By late 2019 it was reported to have about **2 million weekly active users**, far below its 100 million sign-ups. In January 2021 Hike shut down its messaging service completely. Mittal moved the company to gaming and communities, and focused on **Rush**, where people played casual games like ludo and carrom for cash prizes.

chapters.title: The fall
chapters.body: Rush worked. It drew **over 10 million users** and more than $500 million in gross revenue (total money played) over four years. In FY23 Hike's revenue jumped to ₹152 crore, though it still lost ₹147 crore. A US launch began in late 2024. Then, in August 2025, Parliament passed the **Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act** in two days. It banned online money games, whether of skill or chance, with jail terms of up to three years for offering them. Rush's Indian business was gone overnight. In September 2025 Mittal shut Hike entirely, saying a global restart would need "a full recap, a reset that is not the best use of capital or time."

timeline.event: Kavin Bharti Mittal launches Hike Messenger.
Raises $14 M from BSB (Bharti–SoftBank); about 15 M users.
Crosses 100 M registered users and 40 bn messages a month.
Raises $175 M led by Tencent and Foxconn at a $1.4 bn valuation.
Drops the super-app plan; launches separate apps like Hike Sticker Chat.
Shuts down Hike's messaging service; pivots to Rush and other apps.
India passes a law banning online money games.
Mittal shuts down Hike, including its US business.
Hike Messenger Ltd is incorporated in the UK; the brand is later sold to it and the app relaunched.

charts.title: Revenue vs loss in the Rush years
charts.takeaway: Gaming finally brought real revenue, but the company was still spending about ₹2 for every ₹1 it earned.

mistakes.title: Building the last business on a legal grey zone
mistakes.explain: Rush let people play for cash, an area Indian governments had long debated. When the 2025 law banned online money games, **a working business vanished in days**. Mittal could have raised more, but asked if it was worth it. Founders should treat **'the law could change' as a real risk**, not a footnote.

mistakes.title: Taking on WhatsApp's network effect head-on
mistakes.explain: A chat app is only useful if your contacts are on it. WhatsApp already had 100 million+ active Indian users in 2016. Hike's stickers and features were fun, but **people stay where their family is**. Saying 'we don't compete with WhatsApp' did not change **where people actually chatted**.

mistakes.title: Celebrating registered users instead of active users
mistakes.explain: Hike announced 100 million registered users in 2016. By late 2019 it was reported to have about 2 million weekly active users. **Sign-ups flatter; activity tells the truth.** A big registered number can hide a leaking bucket for years and lead to **raising and spending at the wrong scale**.

mistakes.title: Too many directions: super app, then many apps, then games
mistakes.explain: Hike added games, news, coupons and planned payments, then in 2019 broke into separate apps, then shut messaging in 2021 for gaming and Web3. Each pivot was a fresh start with **less money and trust than the last**. Strong founders pivot, but **every pivot resets the clock**.

warningSigns: Is your growth mostly sign-ups, while weekly active users stay flat?
Does your product need users to drag their friends away from an app they already use?
Could a single new law or rule ban your main source of revenue?
Have you pivoted more than twice in three years without one pivot clearly working?
Are you still losing about as much as you earn, even after finding revenue?

lessons.title: Report active users to yourself every week
lessons.detail: Daily and weekly active users are your real score. Put them at the top of every review, above downloads or registrations.

lessons.title: Pick fights where network effects help you
lessons.detail: Start with a group the giant ignores, such as a city, a college or a language, where you can become the default before you go wider.

lessons.title: Map your regulatory risk before you pivot
lessons.detail: Before entering betting, lending, crypto or health, ask a lawyer: what could the government change, and what happens to us if it does?

lessons.title: Give each pivot a clear test and deadline
lessons.detail: Write down what success looks like in six months. If it doesn't happen, decide calmly, instead of drifting into the next idea.

lessons.title: Know when to stop
lessons.detail: Mittal asked if the next climb was worth it and decided it wasn't. Saying no to a reset can protect investors' money and your own years.

quote.text: For the first time in 13 years, my answer is no.
quote.context: Announcing Hike's shutdown in September 2025, after asking whether a global restart was worth it

afterlife.text: Hike shut down in September 2025, including the US business it had launched about nine months earlier. A UK company, Hike Messenger Ltd, was incorporated in London on 30 November 2025, and in 2026 the Hike app was relaunched under it; Mittal said on X that the brand and app had been sold to that company. Challenges to the gaming law moved to the Supreme Court.

disputed.note: Reported by NDTV Gadgets (as cited on Wikipedia); we could not read the original article directly.
TechCrunch says 'gross revenue', meaning money played on the platform, not Hike's own net revenue. Hike's filed FY23 revenue was ₹152 crore.
